title: Local, Global, and Module Scope
learningObjectives: Explain the key vocabulary and behavior covered in this topic.
Distinguish related concepts using a small program example.
Trace how information or execution moves through the example.
Identify a common mistake and explain its consequence.
Apply the concept in a new programming scenario.

understand.concept: Scope describes where a name can be accessed. Local names are available within a function or block according to the language. Global names may be available across a wider program area. Module scope is limited to a module's own code unless names are explicitly exposed. Scope rules differ between languages, so avoid assuming every language handles blocks and declarations identically.
understand.whyItMatters: Scope reduces accidental name collisions and helps control which code can read or change data. Broad shared state can make bugs difficult to locate.
understand.analogy: Imagine rooms in a building: a local name is like an item kept inside one room, a module-level name is available to the team in that room group, and a global name is placed in a shared lobby. Access rules are language-specific and the analogy is imperfect.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy simplifies language-specific rules; verify the actual language semantics when applying the idea.

explain.narrative: A name's scope determines where it can be referenced. Prefer local variables for temporary work and pass data explicitly when possible. Use module-level shared values only when their role is clear. In JavaScript, block-scoped let/const and function-scoped var differ; this lesson focuses on the cross-language idea.

examples.title: Local temporary
examples.code:
function calculate() { const subtotal = 12; return subtotal + 3; }
console.log(calculate());
examples.explanation: subtotal exists inside calculate and is not available outside its function.

examples.title: Same local name in separate functions
examples.explanation: Each function has its own local binding named label.

examples.title: Global access example
examples.explanation: The function reads a wider-scope binding; shared dependencies should be used deliberately.

examples.title: Block scope
examples.code:
if (true) { let message = 'inside'; console.log(message); }
// message is not accessible here
examples.explanation: The let binding is limited to the block in JavaScript.

examples.title: Module boundary
examples.explanation: Module-level names are not automatically global; export/import rules define access.

commonMistakes: Confusing a definition with its execution.
Assuming all languages share the same syntax or scope rules.
Ignoring the difference between visible output and returned data.
Using unclear names or undocumented assumptions.
Skipping checks for unusual or invalid inputs.

guidedTask.title: Guided practice: local, global, and module scope
guidedTask.instructions: Create a small example demonstrating local, global, and module scope. Predict behavior before running, then explain the concept in your own words.
steps: Write a small function focused on one behavior.
Label or document the key concept being demonstrated.
Test at least two cases, including an edge case where relevant.
Explain how the concept affects readability or reliability.

independentTask.title: Independent practice: apply the concept
independentTask.instructions: Build a small scenario-based program that uses this concept deliberately.
requirements: Use clear names and a single focused responsibility where possible.
Include at least two test scenarios.
Show the result and explain it.
Review for unnecessary complexity or hidden side effects.

hints: Write the smallest useful example first.
Trace each input and output carefully.
Test a normal and boundary case.
Use the concept to improve clarity, not to add complexity.

A guarantee that every language works identically
questions.answer: A clearly defined function behavior or boundary

questions.prompt: Why should programmers make assumptions explicit?
options: It helps callers use code correctly and tests verify expectations
It makes code run without inputs
questions.answer: It helps callers use code correctly and tests verify expectations
questions.explanation: Explicit assumptions and checks make behavior easier to review and test.

questions.prompt: What is a good first step when tracing the example?
options: Identify the inputs and follow execution in order
Guess the output and skip the code
questions.answer: Identify the inputs and follow execution in order
questions.explanation: A careful trace follows values and statements step by step.
